lesson.title: Charting the Unknown West After the Louisiana Purchase
lesson.summary: Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the newly purchased Louisiana Territory between 1804 and 1806, producing the first detailed American maps and reports of the land, peoples, and resources west of the Mississippi.
lesson.body:
Even before the Louisiana Purchase was finalized in 1803, President Thomas Jefferson had asked Congress to fund an expedition to explore the Missouri River and search for a water route across the continent to the Pacific Ocean, a long standing ambition of Jefferson's that the sudden acquisition of the Louisiana Territory made both more urgent and more practical. Jefferson chose his personal secretary, Meriwether Lewis, to lead the expedition, and Lewis in turn invited his former army colleague William Clark to share command, forming what the two men called the Corps of Discovery.

The expedition departed from near St. Louis in May 1804 with a party of roughly three dozen soldiers, boatmen, and other members, traveling up the Missouri River through territory the United States had only just claimed and that was, in practical terms, still controlled by dozens of Native nations who had never been consulted about the purchase. Jefferson instructed Lewis and Clark not only to map the land, record its plants, animals, and geography, and search for a practical route to the Pacific, but also to establish diplomatic and commercial relations with Native peoples along the way, treating the expedition as much as a diplomatic mission as a scientific one.

Along the upper Missouri, the expedition wintered among the Mandan and Hidatsa peoples, where they hired a French Canadian fur trader, Toussaint Charbonneau, and his young Shoshone wife, Sacagawea, who joined the party along with their infant son. Sacagawea's knowledge of the Shoshone language and the western terrain, along with her presence, which signaled to other Native groups that the expedition was not a war party, proved crucial when the Corps of Discovery later needed horses and guidance to cross the Rocky Mountains. York, an enslaved man owned by Clark, also traveled with the expedition and took part in the same hunting, portaging, and diplomatic work as the other members, though he received no pay or freedom for it at the time.

After crossing the Rocky Mountains, a passage far harder than Jefferson had hoped, since no easy all water route to the Pacific actually existed, the expedition reached the mouth of the Columbia River and the Pacific Ocean in November 1805, building a winter camp they called Fort Clatsop near present day Astoria, Oregon. They began the return journey the following spring and arrived back in St. Louis in September 1806, having been gone so long that many Americans had assumed the party was lost.

The expedition returned with detailed maps, scientific specimens, and journals that gave the United States its first thorough look at the land, peoples, and resources of the territory Jefferson had purchased from France, strengthening the young nation's claim to the Pacific Northwest and encouraging the fur trade and settlement that followed in subsequent decades. It stands as one of the clearest practical expressions of Jeffersonian Democracy in action, an expanding agrarian republic sending its citizens to survey and claim a continent, even as it set in motion decades of displacement and conflict for the Native nations whose homelands the Corps of Discovery had passed through as guests rather than owners.
